questions.text: During the freezing of a pure metal at its melting point, the latent heat of fusion released represents a release of kinetic (thermal) energy, since the temperature is falling at that moment.
questions.keyExplanation: **P3** | Ch 3 — latent heat = **potential/bonding** energy, and T is constant, not falling. Your exact Quiz I Q4 error.
questions.concise: Latent heat = **potential/bonding** energy, and T is constant during freezing — not falling.
questions.detailed:
**FALSE** on two counts:
1. Latent heat of fusion is the difference in **potential (bonding) energy** between liquid and
   solid — atoms settling into bonded positions release energy from the *bonding* arrangement,
   not from random thermal motion.
2. The temperature is **constant** at T_m during the arrest, not falling. If energy were being
   lost as kinetic (thermal) energy, the temperature would drop.

**The P3 rule, one line:** *latent = hidden = no temperature change.* If T is not changing, the
energy cannot be kinetic. This is your exact Quiz I Q4 error — see Ch. 3 Q21 for the full
treatment.

questions.text: Which of the following is/are true of a unit cell?

statements.text: It is the smallest repeating parallelepiped.
Its opposite faces are parallel and identical.
It possesses the full crystal properties.
Its orientation defines the orientation of the whole crystal.

questions.keyExplanation: **P1** | Ch 2 — all four are valid unit-cell descriptions. Your exact Quiz I Q1 error.
questions.concise: All four are valid unit-cell descriptions.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: smallest repeating parallelepiped.
- Item 2 — TRUE: opposite faces parallel and identical.
- Item 3 — TRUE: possesses the full crystal properties.
- Item 4 — TRUE: its orientation defines the orientation of the whole crystal.

All four correct — this is your exact Quiz I Q1, and the shape that P1 trains you to spot.
See Ch. 2 Q5 for the full discussion.

questions.text: The boundary line separating the *liquid + solid* two-phase field from the *solid* single-phase field is the:
questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 4 — solidus touches the pure **solid** region. Your exact Quiz I Q5 error.
questions.concise: The line touching the pure **solid** field is the solidus.
questions.detailed:
The **solidus** is the boundary below which the alloy is entirely solid — it
separates the (L + α) two-phase field from the **solid** single-phase field.
- (b) the **liquidus** separates (L + α) from the **liquid** field (Q4).
- (c) the solvus separates two solid phases.
- (d) a eutectoid is an invariant *reaction*, not a boundary line.

**The mnemonic that stops this recurring:** *liquidus touches the liquid region; solidus touches
the solid region.* This is your exact Quiz I Q5 error — see Ch. 4 Q16/Q17.

questions.text: The boundary line separating the *liquid + solid* field from the *liquid* single-phase field is the:
questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 4 — liquidus touches the pure **liquid** region. The mirror of Q3; you got this one right in the quiz.
questions.concise: The line touching the pure **liquid** field is the liquidus.
questions.detailed: The liquidus is the boundary separating the liquid + solid field from the single-phase liquid field. **(d)** is correct. Option (a) is the solidus, (b) is the solvus, and (c) is an invariant reaction rather than the liquidus boundary.

questions.text: In BCC iron, the octahedral interstitial void radius is 0.019 nm and the carbon atom radius is 0.08 nm. Carbon nevertheless occupies the octahedral site because:

options.label: a
options.text: it is the site with the fewest nearest neighbours pushing on it (2, not 4), minimising distortion

options.label: b
options.text: it is the larger of the two void types

options.label: c
options.text: it is the only void present in BCC

options.label: d
options.text: carbon cannot enter BCC at all

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 2 — BCC octahedral void is anisotropic (2 close neighbours, not 4).
questions.concise: BCC octahedral site is anisotropic — 2 close neighbours, not 4 — so distortion is minimised.
questions.detailed:
The BCC octahedral site is strongly **anisotropic**: its two nearest neighbours
sit far closer than its four next-nearest. An interstitial there pushes on only **2** atoms
rather than distorting **4** more symmetrically. That shape of distortion — concentrated along
one ⟨100⟩ axis — is energetically cheaper than the symmetric tetrahedral alternative, despite
the nominal radius (0.019 nm vs 0.291R tetrahedral).
- (b) false — the *tetrahedral* void is the larger one in BCC (the reversal of FCC).
- (c) false — BCC has both void types.
- (d) false — carbon does enter BCC (that is what makes martensite, Q29).

See Ch. 2 Q40/Q41 — this is the counter-intuitive centrepiece of the voids topic.

questions.text: For an alloy with C₀ = 30 wt%, a tie line gives Cα = 10 wt% and Cβ = 50 wt%. The weight fractions Wα and Wβ are:
questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 4 — Wα = (30−10)/(50−10) = 20/40 = 0.50; Wβ = (50−30)/40 = 20/40 = 0.50. C₀ = 30 sits exactly midway between Cα and Cβ, so the two fractions are equal. Opposite-arm rule.
questions.detailed:
```
C₀ = 30,  Cα = 10,  Cβ = 50
tie-line length = Cβ − Cα = 50 − 10 = 40

Wα = (C₀ − Cα)/(Cβ − Cα) = (30 − 10)/40 = 20/40 = 0.50
Wβ = (Cβ − C₀)/(Cβ − Cα) = (50 − 30)/40 = 20/40 = 0.50

check: 0.50 + 0.50 = 1.00 ✓
```
**Sanity check:** C₀ = 30 is *exactly* midway between Cα = 10 and Cβ = 50 (because 10 + 50 = 60,
and 60/2 = 30). Whenever C₀ falls exactly midway, the two lever arms are equal and both
fractions are 0.50 — no calculation needed once you spot it. That shortcut is the fastest
possible check on any lever-rule answer. The general opposite-arm rule is in Ch. 4 Q18–Q21.

questions.text: A single crystal is loaded such that the slip-plane normal is at 60° and the slip direction at 60° to the load axis. The Schmid factor is:
questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 6 — m = cos²60° = (0.5)² = 0.25. Note this is *below* the 0.5 maximum.
questions.concise: m = cos²60° = (0.5)² = 0.25 — below the 0.5 maximum.
questions.detailed: The Schmid factor is m = cos φ cos λ = cos60° × cos60° = 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. **(d)** is correct. Option (a), 0.50, is the maximum at 45°/45°; (b) is too large because m cannot exceed 0.5; and (c) is the value near 70°/70°.

questions.assertion: Grain refinement is often used when a design needs higher yield strength without automatically accepting the toughness penalties that can accompany other strengthening treatments.
questions.reason: Smaller grains impede slip transfer and can reduce the effective cleavage unit size, although the toughness response still depends on the alloy, microstructure and loading condition.

options.label: a
options.text: Both the assertion and reason are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.label: b
options.text: Both the assertion and reason are true, but the reason does not correctly explain the assertion.

options.label: c
options.text: The assertion is true, but the reason is false.

options.label: d
options.text: The assertion is false, but the reason is true.

questions.keyExplanation: Both statements are true in their qualified form. Grain refinement raises yield strength by impeding slip transfer and can improve resistance to cleavage, but its effect on toughness is not guaranteed for every alloy or loading condition.
questions.concise: Grain refinement often gives a favorable strength–toughness balance, but no strengthening mechanism has a universal toughness outcome.
questions.detailed: Smaller grains increase the number of boundaries that can impede dislocation motion, raising yield strength through the Hall–Petch effect over its normal range. Refinement can also reduce the size of cleavage facets and improve brittle-fracture resistance. These trends depend on chemistry, phase structure, temperature and fracture mode, so grain refinement should not be described as the only mechanism that can improve both strength and toughness in all cases.

questions.text: Which statement(s) distinguish *normal* from *inverse* segregation?

statements.text: Normal segregation concentrates S, P and C toward the centre and upper portions, forming a V pattern tied to the pipe.
Inverse (Λ) segregation concentrates low-melting elements nearer the outer zones; in extreme cases it reaches the surface as "tin sweat" (exudation).
Inverse segregation is caused by solute-rich liquid being pulled outward through interdendritic channels to feed solidification shrinkage.
Both have exactly the same mechanism.

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 3 — learn the four segregation mechanisms, not four separate facts.
questions.concise: Normal (V) → centre; inverse (Λ) → outward/tin sweat, shrinkage-fed — item 4 says they share a mechanism, which is false.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: normal segregation concentrates S, P, C toward the centre and upper portions,
  a V pattern tied to the pipe.
- Item 2 — TRUE: inverse (Λ) concentrates low-melting elements nearer the outer zones; in
  extreme cases it reaches the surface as "tin sweat" (exudation).
- Item 3 — TRUE: inverse segregation is caused by solute-rich liquid being pulled **outward**
  through interdendritic channels to feed solidification shrinkage.
- Item 4 — FALSE: the two have *opposite* solute transport directions and different mechanisms.

**The four-way to learn as a set:** normal (V, to centre) · inverse (Λ, tin sweat, shrinkage-fed
outward) · gravity (density settling) · micro/coring (inside one grain). See Ch. 3 Q48–Q50.

questions.text: In rimming steel, the reaction FeO + C → Fe + CO↑ produces:

options.label: a
options.text: a fully sound ingot with no defects

options.label: c
options.text: a pure, blowhole-riddled outer rim, a segregated core, and essentially no pipe

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 3 — rimming steel: pure rim + segregated core + **no pipe**.
questions.concise: Rimming: pure rim + segregated core + no pipe.
questions.detailed: Rimming action produces a relatively pure, blowhole-containing outer rim, a segregated core, and little or no shrinkage pipe because CO evolution compensates for shrinkage. **(c)** is correct. Option (a) incorrectly calls the ingot defect-free; (b) describes a shrinkage pipe; and (d) is unrelated martensite.

questions.text: Which of the following are recognised causes of *blowholes* in castings?

statements.text: Gas dissolved during melting (e.g. hydrogen → pinholes in aluminium alloys)
Gas generated at the mould (→ *reeds* in steel after rolling)
Chemical reaction in the melt (CO formation in steel)
Solidification shrinkage

questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 3 — shrinkage (item 4) is a separate defect with a different fix (feeding, not degassing).
questions.concise: Three gas routes (dissolved, mould-generated, reaction) — shrinkage is a separate defect.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: gas dissolved during melting (hydrogen → pinholes in aluminium).
- Item 2 — TRUE: gas generated at the mould (→ *reeds* in steel after rolling).
- Item 3 — TRUE: chemical reaction in the melt (CO formation in steel).
- Item 4 — FALSE: solidification shrinkage is a **separate** defect (sponginess/pipe) with a
  different fix — **feeding**, not **degassing**.

Item 4 is the false member. **The [P2] rule:** *sponginess = shrinkage ⇒ feed it; blowholes =
gas ⇒ degas it.* Confusing the two leads to the wrong remedy. See Ch. 3 Q41–Q43.

questions.text: *Burning* of an alloy during solution treatment is:

options.label: a
options.text: a recoverable loss of ductility from grain-boundary precipitation

options.label: c
options.text: grain-boundary melting caused by crossing the local effective (cored) solidus — permanent, unrecoverable damage

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 4 — burning = crossing the **effective** solidus → permanent.
questions.concise: Burning = crossing the effective solidus → grain-boundary melting → permanent.
questions.detailed: Burning is genuine grain-boundary melting after the local effective (cored) solidus is crossed. It is permanent and unrecoverable. **(c)** is correct. Option (a) describes recoverable overheating; (b) is surface oxidation; and (d) is not a beneficial treatment.

questions.text: The dislocation strain energy per unit length scales as:
questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 5 — E ≈ αGb²; the b² dependence drives both smallest-b selection and dissociation.
questions.concise: E ≈ αGb² — the b² dependence drives smallest-b selection and dissociation.
questions.detailed:
The dislocation strain energy per unit length scales as:
```
E ≈ α G b² ,   α ≈ ½ to 1
```
- (b) Gb has the wrong exponent.
- (c), (d) are not the relation.

Two consequences follow: dislocations always pick the **smallest** available b (Ch. 5 Q32), and
they **dissociate** whenever b₁² + b₂² < b² (Ch. 5 Q35, Q36). The b² is the engine of the
whole chapter.

questions.text: The Burgers vector in FCC is a/2⟨110⟩ with |b| = a/√2. In BCC it is:
questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 5 — BCC a/2⟨111⟩, (√3/2)a vs FCC a/2⟨110⟩, a/√2. Frequently swapped.
questions.detailed: The shortest perfect-dislocation translation in BCC is a/2⟨111⟩, with magnitude (√3/2)a. **(d)** is correct. Option (a) is the FCC a/2⟨110⟩ vector; (b) is a simple-cubic translation; and (c) is a Shockley partial vector.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about an *edge* dislocation is/are correct?

statements.text: It has an extra half-plane of atoms inserted from above.
It has both a shear and a hydrostatic (compression/tension) strain field.
It can climb, which requires vacancy diffusion.
It can cross-slip onto any plane containing its Burgers vector.

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 5 — item 4 is the **screw** dislocation's ability; edge cannot cross-slip.
questions.concise: Edge: extra half-plane, shear + hydrostatic field, can climb — but item 4 is the
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: an extra half-plane of atoms inserted from above.
- Item 2 — TRUE: both a shear and a hydrostatic (compression/tension) strain field.
- Item 3 — TRUE: it can climb, which requires vacancy diffusion.
- Item 4 — FALSE: **cross-slip is the screw dislocation's ability.** An edge has a *unique*
  slip plane (fixed by b and the line direction), so there is nowhere to cross-slip to.

Item 4 is the classic [P2] cross-contamination — the screw's ability transplanted onto the edge.
See Ch. 5 Q20/Q21/Q24 — the complete edge-vs-screw comparison table.

questions.text: Copper (Q_v = 0.9 eV/atom) at 1000 K has n_v/N ≈ 2.9 × 10⁻⁵, i.e. roughly one vacancy in every:
questions.detailed: A vacancy fraction of 2.9 × 10⁻⁵ corresponds to one vacant site in approximately 1/(2.9 × 10⁻⁵) ≈ 34,000 sites. **(a)** is correct. The other options correspond to vacancy fractions one or more orders of magnitude different.

questions.assertion: Real metals yield at stresses three to four orders of magnitude below the theoretical shear strength.
questions.reason: Deformation proceeds by the motion of existing dislocations, breaking and re-forming only one row of bonds at a time, rather than breaking every bond across a whole plane simultaneously.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 5 — the whole reason dislocations must exist.
questions.concise: Dislocation glide breaks one row of bonds at a time — not the whole plane at once.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: real metals yield at stresses three to four orders of magnitude below the
  theoretical shear strength (theory G/30; real G/1000–G/100,000).
- R is TRUE: deformation proceeds by the motion of existing dislocations, breaking and
  re-forming only **one row of bonds at a time** at the core, rather than breaking every bond
  across a whole plane simultaneously.

R correctly explains A. This is the central insight of dislocation theory — think of moving a
carpet wrinkle rather than dragging the whole carpet. See Ch. 5 Q13/Q15/Q17.

questions.text: Match each term to its correct distinguishing question.
tableRows: (a) Which pure phase does this boundary touch?
(b) Does it need exactly one crystal structure, or just "metal + other"?
(c) Is the misorientation random, or a mirror-symmetric reflection?
(d) Is an atom missing from a site, or an extra atom between sites?
questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | All — this is your own confusable-pairs table, in exam format.
questions.concise: This is your own confusable-pairs table, in exam format.
questions.detailed:
| Term pair | Distinguishing question |
|---|---|
| Solid solution / Alloy | (b) Does it need exactly one crystal structure, or just "metal + other"? |
| Liquidus / Solidus | (a) Which pure phase does this boundary touch? |
| Vacancy / Interstitial | (d) Is an atom missing from a site, or an extra atom between sites? |
| Grain / Twin boundary | (c) Is the misorientation random, or a mirror-symmetric reflection? |

Each pair has a **single deciding question**. Learn the questions, not the definitions — then
any arrangement of the question becomes answerable. Full treatments: Ch. 4 Q1/Q2 (SS vs alloy),
Ch. 4 Q16/Q17 (liquidus vs solidus), Ch. 5 Q4/Q5 (vacancy vs interstitial), Ch. 5 Q47/Q48
(grain vs twin).

questions.text: Which set of numbers is correct for FCC?
questions.detailed:
```
FCC:  8 corners × 1/8 + 6 faces × 1/2 = 4 atoms/cell
      CN = 12
      APF = π/(3√2) ≈ 0.74
```
- (b) 2, 8, 0.68 is **BCC**.
- (c) 6, 12, 0.74 is **HCP**.
- (d) mixes FCC's atom count with BCC's CN.

The three sets to have instantly available: **BCC (2, 8, 0.68) · FCC (4, 12, 0.74) · HCP (6,
12, 0.74)**. See Ch. 2 Q7–Q9.

questions.text: Recalescence in a pure-metal cooling curve brings the temperature back up to within about ______ of the true freezing point:
questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 3 — recalescence returns to within ≈0.13 °C.
questions.concise: Recalescence returns the metal to within ~0.13 °C of the true freezing point.
questions.detailed: Recalescence brings the temperature back to within approximately 0.13 °C of the true freezing point. **(b)** is correct. Option (a) is 13 °C, (c) is 1.3 °C, and (d) is 130 °C.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about *heterogeneous nucleation* is/are correct?

statements.text: The critical radius r* is unchanged from the homogeneous case.
The barrier ΔG* is reduced by the shape factor S(ψ).
It requires far less undercooling than homogeneous nucleation.
It makes the critical nucleus smaller.

questions.keyExplanation: **P1/P2** | Ch 3 — heterogeneous changes the **barrier**, not the critical radius. Item 4 is the trap.
questions.concise: Heterogeneous changes the **barrier**, not the critical radius — item 4 is the trap.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: r*_het = r*_hom. The critical radius is **unchanged** — counter-intuitive and
  frequently tested.
- Item 2 — TRUE: the barrier ΔG* is reduced by the shape factor S(ψ) = (2 + cos ψ)(1 − cos ψ)²/4.
- Item 3 — TRUE: it requires far less undercooling than homogeneous nucleation.
- Item 4 — FALSE: it does **not** make the critical nucleus smaller — this is the [P2] trap.

The foreign surface only reduces the *geometry* factor S(ψ), not the underlying r*. Items 1 and
4 are direct opposites, so any option containing item 4 is wrong. See Ch. 3 Q11/Q12.

questions.text: An alloy ingot cast in a metal mould at high pouring temperature typically develops:

options.label: c
options.text: columnar crystals growing almost to the centre

questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 3 — high pouring T in a chill mould → columnar to the centre.
questions.concise: High pouring T in a chill mould → columnar to the centre.
questions.detailed: At high pouring temperature in a metal (chill) mould, columnar crystals can grow almost to the centre. **(c)** is correct. A fine equiaxed structure is favoured by lower pouring temperature; an amorphous structure requires much higher cooling rates; and a single crystal requires seeded growth.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about *killed* and *rimming* steel is/are correct?

statements.text: Killed steel is fully deoxidised with Al, FeSi and FeMn, and freezes with a normal pipe.
Rimming steel is deliberately only partially deoxidised.
Rimming steel's blowholes weld up on hot rolling because CO is non-oxidising, so internal surfaces stay bright.
Rimming steel produces a large shrinkage pipe.

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 3 — item 4 reverses the rimming truth (gas compensates the shrinkage).
questions.concise: Killed = fully deoxidised → pipe; Rimming = partially deoxidised, blowholes weld up — item 4 reverses the rimming truth.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: killed steel is fully deoxidised with Al, FeSi, FeMn, and freezes with a normal pipe.
- Item 2 — TRUE: rimming steel is deliberately only partially deoxidised.
- Item 3 — TRUE: rimming steel's blowholes weld up on hot rolling because CO is non-oxidising,
  so internal surfaces stay bright.
- Item 4 — FALSE: rimming steel produces **essentially no pipe** — the evolved CO gas
  *compensates* the solidification shrinkage (Q10).

Item 4 is the [P2] inversion. See Ch. 3 Q45–Q47.

questions.text: Which Hume-Rothery size rule is correct?

options.label: a
options.text: complete solid solubility requires a size difference above 50%

options.label: b
options.text: complete solid solubility requires a size difference below about 15%

questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 4 — the ~15% Hume-Rothery size limit.
questions.concise: Hume-Rothery size rule: Δr/r < ~15%.
questions.detailed: Complete substitutional solid solubility is favoured when the atomic-size difference is below about 15%. **(b)** is correct. A difference above 50% is far outside the usual limit; size is not irrelevant; and a 1% limit is unnecessarily strict.

questions.text: Electron compounds with e/a = 3:2 adopt which structure?
questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 4 — e/a 3:2 → BCC β; 21:13 → complex cubic γ; 7:4 → HCP ε.
questions.concise: e/a 3:2 → BCC β; 21:13 → complex cubic γ; 7:4 → HCP ε.
questions.detailed: An electron compound with e/a = 3:2 adopts the BCC β structure. **(b)** is correct. The 21:13 ratio corresponds to complex cubic γ, and 7:4 corresponds to HCP ε; FCC is not the 3:2 electron-compound structure.

questions.text: In the lever rule, the weight fraction of a phase is found using:

options.label: a
options.text: the opposite arm of the tie line, divided by the total tie-line length

options.label: c
options.text: the vertical distance between liquidus and solidus

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 4 — always the **opposite** arm.
questions.concise: Always the opposite arm / total length.
questions.detailed:
The lever rule assigns each phase the fraction given by the **opposite** arm:
```
W_L = (C_S − C₀)/(C_S − C_L)      ← solid-side arm
W_α = (C₀ − C_L)/(C_S − C_L)      ← liquid-side arm
```
- (b) the same-side arm gives the *complement* (1 − W) — the classic error.
- (c), (d) are not the rule.

**Sanity check:** the majority phase is always the one C₀ sits nearer. See Ch. 4 Q18–Q21 —
the single most error-prone rule in the course.

questions.assertion: Under non-equilibrium cooling, freezing finishes at a temperature T₄ below the equilibrium finish temperature T₃.
questions.reason: Solid-state diffusion cannot keep the growing solid homogeneous, so the average solid composition lags the equilibrium solidus and a shallower effective solidus is traced out.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

options.label: c
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 4 — the average solid composition lags the equilibrium solidus.
questions.concise: Solid-state diffusion can't keep the solid homogeneous → average composition lags the solidus → shallower effective solidus → T₄ < T₃.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: under non-equilibrium cooling, freezing finishes at T₄ below the equilibrium
  finish temperature T₃.
- R is TRUE: solid-state diffusion cannot keep the growing solid homogeneous, so the average
  solid composition **lags** the equilibrium solidus and a shallower effective solidus is
  traced out.

R correctly explains A. The practical consequence is burning (Q12, Q49): the *effective*
solidus, not the equilibrium one, governs local melting. See Ch. 4 Q33/Q34.

questions.text: In which structure is the *octahedral* void the larger of the two void types?

options.label: c
options.text: both — the octahedral void is always larger

options.label: d
options.text: neither — the two are always equal

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 2 — FCC: octahedral (0.414) is larger. In BCC the *tetrahedral* is larger (0.291) — the reversal.
questions.concise: FCC: octahedral is larger. In BCC the **tetrahedral** is larger — the reversal.
questions.detailed:
| Structure | Larger void |
|---|---|
| **FCC** | **octahedral** (0.414) > tetrahedral (0.225) |
| **BCC** | **tetrahedral** (0.291) > octahedral (0.155) |

- (b) states the BCC numbers but draws the opposite conclusion (0.155 is *not* > 0.291).
- (c), (d) are false.

The BCC/FCC **reversal** is the highest-value fact in the voids topic — students assume
"octahedral is always bigger" from the FCC case. And then see Q5: despite this, carbon in BCC
still chooses the *smaller* octahedral site, for the anisotropy reason. See Ch. 2 Q38–Q41.

questions.text: The tetragonality of martensite follows c/a = 1.000 + 0.045 (wt% C). Which statement(s) correctly explain(s) this?

statements.text: Carbon sits in the anisotropic BCC octahedral site, pushing its two nearest neighbours hard along a ⟨100⟩ direction.
Sufficient carbon preferentially occupying octahedral sites along one axis stretches that axis relative to the other two.
The distortion turns the BCC cell into a body-centred tetragonal (BCT) cell.
It results from the FCC-to-BCC volume change alone.

questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 2 — anisotropic octahedral site → ⟨100⟩ distortion → BCT.
questions.concise: Anisotropic octahedral site → preferential ⟨100⟩ occupation → BCT; not from the FCC→BCC volume change alone.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: carbon sits in the anisotropic BCC octahedral site, pushing its two nearest
  neighbours hard along a ⟨100⟩ direction.
- Item 2 — TRUE: sufficient carbon preferentially occupying octahedral sites along **one** axis
  stretches that axis relative to the other two.
- Item 3 — TRUE: the distortion turns the BCC cell into a body-centred **tetragonal** (BCT) cell.
- Item 4 — FALSE: it does **not** result from the FCC-to-BCC volume change alone — it requires
  the *carbon supersaturation* and its *directional* occupation of one ⟨100⟩ axis. Pure iron
  transforming FCC→BCC stays cubic (c/a = 1.000).

Item 4 is the false member. The formula: **c/a = 1.000 + 0.045 (wt% C)**. See Ch. 2 Q41/Q44.

questions.text: The FCC dissociation a/2[10̄1] → a/6[2 1̄ 1̄] + a/6[11 2̄] produces two Shockley partial dislocations separated by:

options.label: a
options.text: a twin boundary several grains wide

options.label: b
options.text: a ribbon of stacking fault, where ABCABC… is locally disrupted to ABAB…

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 5 — stacking fault = one mis-stacked layer, bounded by two partials; not a twin.
questions.concise: Between the partials: a stacking fault (FCC ABCABC locally becomes HCP-like ABAB).
questions.detailed:
The perfect FCC dislocation a/2[10̄1] dissociates into two Shockley partials:
```
(a/2)[10̄1] → (a/6)[2 1̄ 1̄] + (a/6)[11 2̄]
```
Component-wise, [2, −1, −1] + [1, 1, −2] = [3, 0, −3], so the partials sum to (a/2)[1, 0, −1], exactly the parent Burgers vector. The two partials enclose a ribbon of stacking fault, where the FCC ABCABC… sequence is locally disrupted into ABAB… stacking. **(b)** is correct. This vector form also matches the corrected dissociation in Chapter 5.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about stacking-fault energy is/are correct?

statements.text: Low-SFE metals such as brass and austenitic stainless steel have wide partial ribbons.
Wide ribbons make cross-slip difficult, because the partials must first constrict.
Low-SFE metals therefore work-harden faster and retain a planar dislocation structure.
Aluminium has a low stacking-fault energy.

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 5 — item 4 is false: Al has **high** SFE (narrow ribbons).
questions.concise: Low SFE → wide ribbons → hard cross-slip → faster work hardening; but Al has **high** SFE, not low.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: low-SFE metals (brass, austenitic stainless) have wide partial ribbons.
- Item 2 — TRUE: wide ribbons make cross-slip difficult — the partials must first **constrict**
  into a perfect dislocation before switching planes.
- Item 3 — TRUE: low-SFE metals therefore work-harden **faster** and retain a planar
  dislocation structure.
- Item 4 — FALSE: **aluminium has a high stacking-fault energy** (narrow ribbons, easy
  cross-slip, slow work hardening). Al is the standard *high*-SFE example.

Item 4 is the [P2] trap — Al is always quoted as the *contrast* to brass and austenitic
stainless. The full chain: low γ_sf → wide ribbon → cross-slip blocked → faster hardening →
planar structure. See Ch. 5 Q38–Q40.

questions.text: For a single crystal with τ_crss = 1 MPa oriented at φ = λ = 45°, σ_y = 2 MPa. Oriented instead at φ = λ = 70°, σ_y ≈ 8.5 MPa. The increase is due purely to:

options.label: a
options.text: orientation, since τ_crss is an intrinsic material property independent of loading direction

options.label: b
options.text: a change in the crystal's composition

options.label: d
options.text: a change in the Burgers vector

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 6 — τ_crss is intrinsic; only the Schmid factor changes.
questions.concise: Purely orientation — τ_crss is intrinsic; only the Schmid factor changes.
questions.detailed:
```
τ_crss = σ_y · m      →      σ_y = τ_crss / m

45°:  m = 0.5   →  σ_y = 1/0.5   = 2 MPa
70°:  m = 0.117 →  σ_y = 1/0.117 ≈ 8.5 MPa
```
τ_crss is unchanged — it is an intrinsic material property set by crystal structure, bonding,
temperature and purity. Only the **Schmid factor** m changed with orientation, producing a ~4×
difference in the applied yield stress.
- (b), (c), (d) would all change τ_crss itself, which did not happen.

This is the practical origin of texture effects in forming and of single-crystal turbine-blade
orientation. See Ch. 6 Q18–Q21.

questions.text: HCP metals are markedly less ductile than FCC metals as polycrystals because:

statements.text: HCP has only 3 basal slip systems
the von Mises criterion requires 5 independent slip systems for arbitrary shape change
twinning supplies the extra deformation modes HCP needs
HCP has a lower packing factor than FCC

questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 6 — the von Mises 5-system criterion explains HCP brittleness.
questions.concise: HCP has 3 basal systems < 5 needed (von Mises); twinning supplies extra modes — but HCP does **not** have a lower packing factor than FCC.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: HCP has only 3 basal slip systems.
- Item 2 — TRUE: the von Mises criterion requires **5** independent slip systems for arbitrary
  shape change of a grain constrained by its neighbours.
- Item 3 — TRUE: twinning supplies the extra deformation modes HCP needs.
- Item 4 — FALSE: HCP and FCC have the **identical** packing factor, 0.74. What differs is the
  *number of slip systems*, not the packing.

Item 4 is the [P2] trap — identical packing, different ductility. This is the single most
important link between Ch. 2 and Ch. 6: **ductility follows the slip-system count, not the
packing density.** See Ch. 2 Q20 and Ch. 6 Q11/Q12.

questions.text: The *Cottrell atmosphere* is:

options.label: b
options.text: a precipitate at a grain boundary

options.label: c
options.text: interstitial solute atoms (C, N) clustering in the tensile zone below an edge dislocation's extra half-plane, pinning it

questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 6 — interstitials sit in the tensile (expanded) zone.
questions.concise: Cottrell atmosphere = C, N in the tensile zone below the extra half-plane, pinning it.
questions.detailed: A Cottrell atmosphere is a cluster of interstitial solute atoms, especially C or N, in the tensile region below the extra half-plane of an edge dislocation. The solutes pin the dislocation. **(c)** is correct. Option (a) is a vacancy cloud; (b) is a grain-boundary precipitate; and (d) is a stacking-fault ribbon.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about *strain ageing* is/are correct?

statements.text: Solute diffuses back to stationary dislocations after unloading, re-forming Cottrell atmospheres.
On reloading the yield point reappears, often at a higher stress than before.
Strength and hardness increase while ductility and toughness decrease.
It permanently eliminates the yield-point phenomenon.

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 6 — item 4 reverses the truth; ageing *restores* the yield point.
questions.concise: Solute re-pins on rest → yield point returns at higher stress, strength up ductility down — item 4 says it *eliminates* the yield point, which is the reverse.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: solute diffuses back to stationary dislocations after unloading, re-forming
  Cottrell atmospheres.
- Item 2 — TRUE: on reloading the yield point reappears, often at a higher stress than before.
- Item 3 — TRUE: strength and hardness increase while ductility and toughness decrease.
- Item 4 — FALSE: strain ageing **restores** (re-establishes) the yield-point phenomenon; it
  does **not** permanently eliminate it.

Item 4 is the [P2] inversion. (The industrial treatment that *does* eliminate the yield point
is **temper rolling / skin-pass**, not ageing.) See Ch. 6 Q35–Q37.

questions.text: The Hall–Petch slope k_y represents:

options.label: c
options.text: the locking parameter — how effectively grain boundaries block slip transmission

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 7 — k_y = locking parameter, σ₀ = friction stress, d = grain diameter.
questions.concise: k_y = locking parameter (boundary strength); σ₀ = friction stress; d = grain diameter.
questions.detailed:
In σ_y = σ₀ + k_y d^(−1/2):
- **k_y** = locking parameter — the slope, how effectively boundaries block slip.
- **σ₀** = lattice friction stress — the intercept.
- **d** = average grain diameter.
- (d) the strain-hardening exponent is n in σ = Kεⁿ (Ch. 7 Q11).

Three-way confusion risk — say the equation aloud to name each symbol. See Ch. 7 Q13–Q15.

questions.text: A metal has σ₀ = 100 MPa and k_y = 0.7 MPa·mm^(1/2). If the grain diameter is d = 0.01 mm, the yield strength is:
questions.keyExplanation: d = 0.01 mm gives d^(−1/2) = 10 mm^(−1/2). Therefore σ_y = 100 + 0.7 × 10 = 107 MPa, so option (a) is correct.
questions.detailed:
Using the supplied units consistently:
```
d = 0.01 mm
 d^(−1/2) = 1/√0.01 = 10 mm^(−1/2)
k_y d^(−1/2) = 0.7 MPa·mm^(1/2) × 10 mm^(−1/2) = 7 MPa
σ_y = σ₀ + k_y d^(−1/2) = 100 + 7 = 107 MPa
```
Therefore **(a)** is correct. Option (b), 700 MPa, is not the Hall–Petch result; (c), 100.7 MPa, misapplies the grain-size term; and (d), 170 MPa, does not follow from the stated data. The key had incorrectly selected (d).

questions.text: Which statement(s) about *precipitation hardening* is/are correct?

statements.text: In the underaged condition, fine coherent precipitates are cut by dislocations.
In the overaged condition, precipitates become incoherent and too strong to shear, so dislocations bow around them (Orowan looping), leaving loops.
Overaged alloys are weaker than peak-aged ones because coarsening increases the inter-particle spacing, lowering the bowing stress.
Overaged alloys are weaker because each particle becomes softer.

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 7 — item 4 is false: overaged particles are *harder*; the weakness comes from **spacing**.
questions.concise: Underaged = cutting; overaged = Orowan looping, weaker due to **spacing** — item 4 says particles become *softer*, which is false (they get harder).
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: underaged, fine coherent precipitates are cut by dislocations.
- Item 2 — TRUE: overaged, precipitates become incoherent and too strong to shear, so
  dislocations bow around them (Orowan looping), leaving loops.
- Item 3 — TRUE: overaged alloys are weaker than peak-aged ones because coarsening increases
  the inter-particle spacing λ, lowering the bowing stress (τ ∝ Gb/λ).
- Item 4 — FALSE: overaged particles are individually **harder**, not softer. The weakness comes
  from the **spacing**, not from particle softness.

Item 4 is the [P2] trap — the counter-intuitive centrepiece of Ch. 7. **Controlling variable =
spacing, not hardness.** See Ch. 7 Q33–Q35.

questions.text: The correct order of the ageing precipitate sequence is:
questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 7 — increasing size, decreasing coherency.
questions.concise: Increasing size, decreasing coherency.
questions.detailed:
```
GP zones → coherent → semi-coherent → incoherent
(size increases, coherency breaks down)
```
- (b) is exactly reversed.
- (c), (d) are scrambled.

As particles grow, the lattice mismatch can no longer be accommodated elastically, so misfit
dislocations appear (semi-coherent), then coherency is lost entirely. See Ch. 7 Q31.

questions.text: Match the annealing stage to its effect.
tableRows: (b) relieves internal stress; no change in grain shape or strength
(c) lowers strength if overdone (Hall–Petch in reverse)
questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 7 — recovery (no grain change) → recrystallisation (strength drops) → grain growth.
questions.concise: Recovery = no grain change · Recrystallisation = strength drops, ductility restored · Grain growth = lowers strength if overdone.
questions.detailed:
| Stage | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Recovery** | (b) relieves internal stress; no change in grain shape or strength |
| **Recrystallisation** | (a) strength drops sharply, ductility restored |
| **Grain growth** | (c) lowers strength if overdone (Hall–Petch in reverse) |

The sequence is fixed: **recovery → recrystallisation → grain growth**, in order of increasing
temperature/time, each driven by reducing stored energy. See Ch. 7 Q39.

questions.text: In Fick's second law solution, the diffusion penetration depth scales as √(Dt). Doubling the case depth at fixed temperature therefore requires:
questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 8 — depth ∝ √(Dt): 2× depth = 4× time.
questions.concise: Depth ∝ √(Dt): 2× depth = 4× time.
questions.detailed: Diffusion depth scales as √t, so the time required scales as the square of depth. Doubling the depth therefore requires 4× the time. **(d)** is correct. Option (a) would give only √2 times the depth; (b) and (c) are inconsistent with the square-law scaling.

questions.text: For a carburizing problem with C₀ = 0.05, C_s = 1.0, C_x = 0.4 wt% C, the normalised concentration is 0.368, giving erf(z) = 0.632 and z ≈ 0.64. With x = 0.6 mm and D = 1 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s, t ≈:
questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 8 — the full carburizing worked example.
questions.concise: The full carburizing worked example — 2.2 × 10⁴ s ≈ 6.1 h.
questions.detailed: The worked carburising example gives t ≈ 2.2 × 10⁴ s. **(b)** is correct. Option (a), 2.2 × 10² s, is 100 times too short; (c), 2.2 × 10³ s, is ten times too short; and (d), 2.2 × 10⁵ s, is ten times too long. Convert x to metres before squaring it.

questions.text: The correct ordering of diffusivity, fastest to slowest, is:

options.label: a
options.text: free surface > grain boundary > bulk lattice

options.label: b
options.text: bulk lattice > grain boundary > free surface

options.label: c
options.text: grain boundary > free surface > bulk lattice

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 8 — surface > grain boundary > bulk.
questions.concise: Surface > grain boundary > bulk — memorise this order.
questions.detailed:
```
free surface   fastest   (most open, lowest coordination)
grain boundary medium    (disordered)
bulk lattice   slowest   (dense, ordered, highest Q_d)
```
- (b) is exactly reversed.
- (c) has the top two swapped.
- (d) is false.

The reason is **order**: more disordered and open → lower activation energy → faster. See
Ch. 8 Q32/Q33.

questions.assertion: Carbon diffuses faster in BCC α-Fe than in FCC γ-Fe, even though γ-Fe has a much higher carbon solubility.
questions.reason: BCC has the lower atomic packing factor (0.68 vs 0.74), which gives easier atomic passage even though the individual BCC voids are smaller.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

options.label: c
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 8/2 — solubility ≠ diffusivity; lower APF means faster diffusion.
questions.concise: Solubility ≠ diffusivity: BCC's lower APF (0.68) means faster diffusion despite smaller voids and lower solubility.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: carbon diffuses faster in BCC α-Fe than in FCC γ-Fe, even though γ-Fe has a much
  higher carbon solubility.
- R is TRUE: BCC has the lower atomic packing factor (0.68 vs 0.74), which gives easier atomic
  passage even though the individual BCC voids are smaller.

R correctly explains A. **Two properties, opposite directions:**
```
SOLUBILITY:  FCC >> BCC   (bigger voids in FCC)
DIFFUSIVITY: BCC > FCC    (lower APF)
```
Solubility is about void **size**; diffusivity is about **packing** and barrier height. See
Ch. 2 Q42 and Ch. 8 Q34.

questions.text: On an Arrhenius plot of ln D against 1/T, the line for interstitial diffusion lies above (and is shallower than) that for substitutional diffusion because:

options.label: a
options.text: interstitial diffusion has a higher Q_d

options.label: c
options.text: interstitial diffusion is slower at high temperature

options.label: d
options.text: interstitial diffusion has a lower activation energy Q_d and is faster at every temperature

questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 8 — slope = −Q_d/R; shallower = lower Q_d.
questions.concise: Shallower slope = lower Q_d = faster at every T.
questions.detailed: Interstitial diffusion generally has a lower activation energy than substitutional diffusion and is faster at a given temperature in the usual comparison. **(d)** states this correctly. Option (a) reverses the activation-energy ordering; (b) incorrectly makes the Arrhenius lines parallel; and (c) incorrectly claims interstitial diffusion is slower at high temperature.

questions.text: Which of the following is/are correct statements about Fick's first law, J = −D dC/dx?

statements.text: The negative sign indicates diffusion down the concentration gradient.
It applies at steady state, where the concentration profile does not change with time.
J has units of flux (atoms per unit area per unit time).
It applies to non-steady-state carburizing.

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 8 — item 4 is a *second-law* problem.
questions.concise: Down-the-gradient, steady state, flux units — item 4 is a *second-law* problem.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: the negative sign indicates diffusion **down** the concentration gradient.
- Item 2 — TRUE: it applies at steady state, where the profile does not change with time.
- Item 3 — TRUE: J has units of flux (atoms per unit area per unit time).
- Item 4 — FALSE: **non-steady-state carburizing is a Fick's second law problem**, not first law.

Item 4 is the classic cross-over between the two laws. And note the **[P3]** angle on item 1:
the minus sign is a **direction convention**, not a statement about heat or energy — do not
read "minus" as "thermal". See Ch. 8 Q9–Q13.

questions.text: Which of the following correctly matches the iron allotropy transformation temperatures?
questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 2 — the allotropy sequence.
questions.concise: α BCC → γ FCC → δ BCC → liquid.
questions.detailed:
```
α-Fe (BCC)  --912 °C-->   γ-Fe (FCC, austenite)
γ-Fe (FCC)  --1394 °C-->  δ-Fe (BCC)
δ-Fe (BCC)  --1538 °C-->  liquid
```
- (b) reverses the α/γ order.
- (c) swaps the 912 and 1394 °C temperatures.
- (d) puts δ at the wrong end.

The pattern: **BCC → FCC → BCC → liquid**. Iron is BCC at both the lowest and highest solid
temperatures, and FCC (austenite) only in between — the physical basis of every steel heat
treatment. See Ch. 2 Q46.

questions.text: Which statements are true of metallic bonding and its macroscopic consequences?

statements.text: Valence electrons are delocalised across the metallic structure.
The bonding interaction is generally non-directional.
Mobile electrons contribute to metals’ high electrical and thermal conductivity.
Electrical conduction occurs mainly through ions hopping between fixed lattice sites rather than through electronic states.

questions.keyExplanation: Statements 1–3 are correct. Statement 4 describes neither the main conduction mechanism in metals nor the role of delocalised electrons.
questions.concise: Delocalised electrons explain the non-directional metallic bond and much of metals’ electrical and thermal conductivity.
questions.detailed: Metallic bonding is commonly modeled as positive ion cores embedded in delocalised valence electrons. The bonding is non-directional compared with covalent bonding, and mobile electronic states carry charge and energy. Ionic hopping is not the dominant ordinary electrical-conduction mechanism in metals.

questions.assertion: A cored, as-cast alloy must never be homogenised or solution-treated right up against its equilibrium solidus temperature.
questions.reason: Coring concentrates low-melting material at grain boundaries, so the effective solidus that actually governs local melting sits below the equilibrium solidus; crossing it causes burning.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

options.label: d
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Ch 4 — the effective (cored) solidus governs, not the equilibrium one.
questions.concise: Coring puts low-melting material at boundaries → effective solidus below equilibrium → crossing it causes burning.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: a cored, as-cast alloy must never be homogenised or solution-treated right up
  against its equilibrium solidus temperature.
- R is TRUE: coring concentrates low-melting material at grain boundaries, so the **effective**
  solidus that actually governs local melting sits **below** the equilibrium solidus; crossing
  it causes burning.

R correctly explains A. The safe practice is to work from the **effective** solidus upward as
coring is removed, never to aim at the equilibrium line. This is the single most practically
important rule in Ch. 4 — see Q12 and Ch. 4 Q38–Q42.

questions.text: Of the following, which cooling rate most closely corresponds to the formation of a **metallic glass**?
questions.keyExplanation: — | Ch 3 — ~10⁷ °C/s → metallic glass; 10⁵–10⁶ → splat quench/metastable; 10³–10⁴ → RSP; 10² → chill casting.
questions.concise: ~10⁷ °C/s → metallic glass.
questions.detailed:
The cooling-rate spectrum:
```
~10² °C/s         chill casting (fine grains)
~10³–10⁴ °C/s     rapid solidification processing (very fine)
~10⁵–10⁶ °C/s     splat quenching (metastable phases)
~10⁷ °C/s         METALLIC GLASS (no time for any nucleation)
```
- (a) 10² gives a fine chill-cast grain structure, still crystalline.
- (b) 10³–10⁴ gives very fine grains (RSP), still crystalline.
- (c) 10⁵–10⁶ gives metastable phases (splat quench), still crystalline.

To form a glass you must bypass nucleation *entirely* — that needs the extreme end of the
spectrum, ~10⁷ °C/s. See Ch. 3 (cooling-rate spectrum).

questions.text: Which of the following correctly pairs a type of atomic bonding with its structural origin and its mechanical/electrical consequence?

options.label: a
options.text: Covalent — electrons shared in a directionally saturated network — diamond has coordination 12 and conducts electricity like a metal

options.label: b
options.text: Ionic — electrons transferred from cation to anion — the bond has no preferred direction, so ionic crystals are ductile

options.label: c
options.text: van der Waals — unsaturated primary bonds between adjacent atoms — these hold the graphite layers together and make graphite hard

options.label: d
options.text: Metallic — a shared cloud of delocalised valence electrons — the bond is non-directional, giving both high electrical conductivity and ductility

questions.keyExplanation: — | Metallic bonding is a non-directional shared electron sea, which explains both conductivity and ductility, whereas diamond is CN 4, ionic crystals are brittle and van der Waals bonding is secondary.
questions.concise: The metallic bond is a non-directional shared electron sea, and that single fact explains both the conductivity and the ductility.
questions.detailed: Metallic bonding consists of delocalised valence electrons shared across the metal. Its non-directional character helps explain both high electrical conductivity and ductility. **(d)** is correct. Option (a) misdescribes diamond's coordination and conductivity; (b) incorrectly calls ionic crystals ductile; and (c) confuses strong in-plane covalent bonding in graphite with weak interlayer van der Waals bonding.

questions.text: A lead–tin alloy containing 30 wt% Sn is cooled under equilibrium conditions to just below 183 °C. The eutectic composition is 61.9 wt% Sn and the maximum solubility of Sn in α is 18.3 wt%. The mass fractions of primary (proeutectic) α and of the eutectic constituent are:
questions.detailed:
```
just above 183 °C:  C_L = 61.9,  C_α = 18.3,  C₀ = 30   (wt% Sn)
W(primary α) = (61.9 − 30)/(61.9 − 18.3) = 31.9/43.6 = 0.73
W(eutectic)  = 1 − 0.73 = 0.27
```
The lever arm for primary α is taken from C₀ **to the eutectic composition**, because that is the liquid composition sitting on the tie line just above the invariant temperature.
- (b), (c) fail the arithmetic or reverse the arms.
- (d) is the trap: 30 < 61.9 wt% Sn makes this **hypo**eutectic, so there is a primary α but **no primary β**.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about slip in the three common crystal structures is/are correct?

statements.text: In FCC metals, slip occurs on the close-packed {111} planes along the close-packed ⟨110⟩ directions, giving 4 planes × 3 directions = 12 slip systems.
In BCC metals, the close-packed direction is ⟨111⟩ and slip most often takes place on the {110} family of planes.
In HCP metals, the close-packed directions lie within the basal plane, so basal slip supplies only 3 independent slip systems.
FCC has the longest Burgers vector of the three (a/√2 > (√3/2)a), which is why its lattice friction stress is the highest.

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Items 1–3 give the correct slip systems, while item 4 reverses the Burgers-vector sizes, since a/√2 = 0.707a is shorter than BCC's (√3/2)a = 0.866a.
questions.concise: Items 1–3 give the correct slip systems; item 4 reverses the Burgers-vector magnitudes.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: FCC is {111}⟨110⟩, 4 planes × 3 directions = 12 systems.
- Item 2 — TRUE: BCC is ⟨111⟩ close-packed direction, usually on {110} (also {112}, {123}).
- Item 3 — TRUE: HCP close-packed directions lie in the basal plane, so only 3 independent basal systems exist — hence the von Mises shortage of Q63.
- Item 4 — FALSE: FCC |b| = a/√2 ≈ 0.707a, BCC |b| = (√3/2)a ≈ 0.866a — FCC's Burgers vector is the **shortest** of the three, one reason FCC metals slip so easily.

**The [P2] pair to state cold:** FCC {111}⟨110⟩ (plane, then direction) vs BCC {110}⟨111⟩ — they are always swapped under exam pressure.

questions.text: Equilibrium cooling data for a hypoeutectic binary alloy (the primary phase is α), given as temperature → weight fraction of liquid W_L: 700 °C → 1.00; 690 °C → 1.00; 680 °C → 0.85; 650 °C → 0.60; 620 °C → 0.35; 590 °C → 0.20; 578 °C → 0.15; 577 °C → 0.00. Which reading of the data is correct?

options.label: a
options.text: The liquidus lies between 690 °C and 680 °C; the drop at 577 °C is the eutectic reaction, which converts the final 0.15 of liquid, leaving 0.85 primary α plus 0.15 eutectic

options.label: b
options.text: The alloy is of eutectic composition, since all the liquid disappears at a single temperature

options.label: c
options.text: The liquidus is 700 °C, and the eutectic reaction converts 0.35 of the remaining liquid

options.label: d
options.text: The solidus is 590 °C, where the last of the liquid is consumed

questions.keyExplanation: — | W_L first falls below 1.00 between 690 °C and 680 °C, and the drop from 0.15 to zero at 577 °C is the eutectic reaction, giving 0.85 primary α + 0.15 eutectic.
questions.concise: W_L first falls below 1.00 between 690 °C and 680 °C, and the last 0.15 of liquid reacts isothermally at 577 °C.
questions.detailed: The liquid fraction remains 1.00 at 700 °C and 690 °C, then first falls at 680 °C, so the liquidus lies between 690 °C and 680 °C. At 577 °C the final 0.15 liquid undergoes the eutectic reaction, leaving 0.85 primary α plus 0.15 eutectic. **(a)** is correct. This is a hypoeutectic alloy, not a eutectic-composition alloy.

questions.assertion: The equilibrium concentration of vacancies in a metal rises exponentially with temperature, and vacancies are the vehicles by which atoms move during self-diffusion.
questions.reason: Self-diffusion requires both the formation of a vacancy (energy Q_f) and its migration into a neighbouring site (energy Q_m), so the measured activation energy is Q_d = Q_f + Q_m.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

options.label: c
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

questions.keyExplanation: — | Q_d = Q_f + Q_m shows both the exponential temperature dependence of the vacancy concentration and the fact that vacancies carry the diffusion.
questions.concise: n_v/N = exp(−Q_f/kT) gives the exponential rise, and Q_d = Q_f + Q_m proves vacancies are the diffusing vehicles.
questions.detailed:
- A is TRUE: the equilibrium vacancy concentration is n_v/N = exp(−Q_f/kT) — exponential in 1/T — and atoms can only move by exchanging with a vacant site.
- R is TRUE: an atom must first **create** a vacancy (Q_f) and then **move** into it (Q_m), so the Arrhenius slope measured experimentally is Q_d = Q_f + Q_m.

R correctly explains A — the macroscopic activation energy contains the vacancy-formation term precisely because diffusion is vacancy-mediated:
```
D = D₀ exp(−Q_d/RT),   Q_d = Q_f + Q_m
```

questions.text: Match each heat-treatment operation to the condition it must satisfy.
tableRows: (a) lies above the recrystallisation temperature, replacing the deformed structure by new strain-free grains
(b) lies between the solvus and the low-melting eutectic (incipient-melting) temperature
(c) is carried out below the solvus, growing fine precipitates from a supersaturated solid solution
(d) is held just below the effective (cored) solidus, for a time set by the square of the diffusion distance
questions.keyExplanation: — | Solution treatment sits between solvus and incipient melting, ageing below the solvus, homogenisation below the effective solidus and annealing above the recrystallisation temperature.
questions.concise: Solution treatment sits between solvus and incipient melting, ageing below the solvus, homogenisation below the effective solidus, annealing above the recrystallisation temperature.
questions.detailed:
- **1 → (b):** solution treatment must be **above the solvus** (single phase, all precipitate dissolved) but **below the low-melting eutectic** or incipient melting burns the part.
- **2 → (c):** ageing is **below the solvus**, where the precipitate is stable and grows from the supersaturated solution trapped by the quench.
- **3 → (d):** homogenisation works **just below the effective (cored) solidus**, and the time needed scales with the **square** of the diffusion distance across the dendrites.
- **4 → (a):** a full anneal is **above the recrystallisation temperature**, replacing the deformed structure by new strain-free grains.

Option (c) swaps the anneal and homogenisation conditions — the two operations that most often get transposed.

questions.text: The shear stress needed to drive dislocations through a forest of density ρ is approximated by τ ≈ Gb√ρ. With G = 40 GPa and b = 0.25 nm, the stresses at ρ = 10¹² m⁻² and ρ = 10¹⁴ m⁻² are, respectively:
questions.keyExplanation: — | τ = Gb√ρ = (40 × 10⁹ × 0.25 × 10⁻⁹)√ρ = 10√ρ, giving 10 MPa at ρ = 10¹² m⁻² and 100 MPa at ρ = 10¹⁴ m⁻².
questions.concise: τ = Gb√ρ = 10√ρ, giving 10 MPa at ρ = 10¹² m⁻² and 100 MPa at ρ = 10¹⁴ m⁻².
questions.detailed:
```
Gb  = 40 × 10⁹ Pa × 0.25 × 10⁻⁹ m = 10 N/m
ρ = 10¹² m⁻²  → √ρ = 10⁶ m⁻¹  → τ = 10 × 10⁶ Pa = 10⁷ Pa = 10 MPa
ρ = 10¹⁴ m⁻²  → √ρ = 10⁷ m⁻¹  → τ = 10 × 10⁷ Pa = 10⁸ Pa = 100 MPa
```
The key point is the **square root**: a 100-fold rise in dislocation density buys only a **10-fold** rise in flow stress — which is exactly why strain hardening alone can never reach the theoretical strength.
- (a), (b), (d) all fail the √ρ arithmetic by an order of magnitude or more — only (c) keeps the 10√ρ scaling straight.

questions.text: Which combination of a metallurgical condition, the treatment applied to it, and the strengthening mechanism that results is completely correct?

options.label: a
options.text: Cored as-cast dendritic structure — homogenisation just below the effective solidus — the alloy is then strengthened mainly by Hall–Petch grain refinement

options.label: b
options.text: Supersaturated solid solution — solution treat above the solvus, quench, then age below the solvus — fine coherent precipitates are cut by moving dislocations

options.label: c
options.text: Overaged alloy — ageing continued past the peak — strength keeps rising because each coarsened particle is individually harder

options.label: d
options.text: Heavily deformed single crystal — cold work — the strength rise comes from Hall–Petch blocking of dislocations at grain boundaries

questions.keyExplanation: — | Only option (b) chains a supersaturated solution formed above the solvus to ageing below the solvus, where fine coherent particles are cut by dislocations.
questions.concise: Only option (b) correctly chains the phase-diagram route to the precipitation-cutting mechanism.
questions.detailed:
- (a) false — homogenisation removes coring; it does not grain-refine, and the coarse as-cast grains it inherits are normally **coarsened**, not refined.
- (c) false — past the peak, strength **falls**: coarsening opens up the interparticle spacing, so the Orowan bowing stress drops (the particles themselves get harder, not softer).
- (d) false — a **single crystal** has no grain boundaries, so Hall–Petch blocking cannot contribute at all; its strength rise is pure strain hardening.

Each wrong option breaks one link of the three-part chain: condition → treatment → mechanism.

questions.text: Vacancies introduced by severe cold work raise the diffusion coefficient of a metal above its equilibrium value, and the coefficient returns to the equilibrium value only once those excess vacancies have annealed out at sinks.
questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | Cold work generates excess vacancies above the equilibrium value, so D is enhanced until those vacancies anneal out at sinks.
questions.concise: Cold work generates excess vacancies above the equilibrium value, so D is enhanced until those vacancies anneal out at sinks.
questions.detailed:
**TRUE**, in two steps:
1. The diffusion coefficient is D ∝ (n_v/N) × (jump rate). Severe deformation generates **non-equilibrium vacancies** (jogs on moving dislocations multiply them far above n_v/N = exp(−Q_f/kT)), so the measured D is **higher** than the equilibrium value at that temperature.
2. Those excess vacancies are unstable: they migrate to sinks (surfaces, grain boundaries, dislocations) and are annihilated, so D **falls back** to the equilibrium value — which is why deformation-enhanced diffusion and strain-ageing effects decay on holding.

**The [P2] pair:** *equilibrium vacancies* (fixed by temperature alone) vs *quenched-in/deformation vacancies* (fixed by thermal or mechanical history) — only the second kind ever changes D away from its equilibrium value.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about the heat treatment of a precipitation-hardening alloy is/are correct?

statements.text: The phase diagram must show a maximum solid solubility that decreases with temperature, so that a quench from the single-phase field traps a supersaturated solid solution.
The solution-treatment temperature must lie above the solvus yet below any low-melting eutectic, to avoid incipient melting.
Ageing is carried out above the solvus, so that the precipitate phase is stable while it grows.
The quench must be fast enough to suppress precipitation during cooling to room temperature.

questions.keyExplanation: — | Item 3 is false: ageing must be below the solvus, where the precipitate is stable; items 1, 2 and 4 are the standard requirements.
questions.concise: Items 1, 2 and 4 are the classic requirements; item 3 is false because ageing must be below the solvus.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: solubility that **falls with temperature** is what lets the quench trap a supersaturated solution.
- Item 2 — TRUE: above the solvus but below any low-melting eutectic — crossing the eutectic causes incipient melting/burning.
- Item 3 — FALSE: **above** the solvus the precipitate simply **dissolves**; ageing must be carried out **below** the solvus, where the precipitate is the stable phase.
- Item 4 — TRUE: cool too slowly and the equilibrium precipitate forms coarse and useless during the cool itself.

questions.text: Which combination of point defect, host structure and measurable consequence is correct?

options.label: a
options.text: Schottky defect in NaCl — a cation–anion vacancy pair — the crystal density increases

options.label: b
options.text: Frenkel defect in AgCl — an Ag⁺ ion displaced from its lattice site into an interstitial — the crystal density is unchanged

options.label: c
options.text: Substitutional solute much smaller than the solvent — an atom on a regular lattice site — no strain field is created in the matrix

options.label: d
options.text: Schottky defect in pure copper — a paired cation and anion vacancy — copper is converted into an ionic structure

questions.keyExplanation: **P2** | A Frenkel defect conserves both mass and volume so the density is unchanged, whereas a Schottky defect removes mass and lowers density.
questions.concise: Frenkel defects conserve both mass and volume, so density is unchanged; Schottky defects remove mass and lower density.
questions.detailed:
- (a) false — a Schottky pair **removes** atoms from the crystal with no volume compensation, so the density **falls**.
- (b) TRUE — the ion merely moves from a site to a void inside the same crystal: same mass, same volume, same density.
- (c) false — any size mismatch creates a coherency strain field, and those strain fields are precisely what makes solid-solution strengthening work.
- (d) false — pure copper has no cations and anions; a Schottky defect needs an ionic compound.

**The [P2] rule:** *Schottky = missing pair = density down; Frenkel = displaced ion = density unchanged.*

questions.text: A single crystal of a metal with τ_crss = 2 MPa is oriented at φ = 20° and λ = 60°. A polycrystal of the same metal has σ₀ = 50 MPa, k_y = 0.7 MPa·mm^(1/2) and grain diameter d = 0.0025 mm. The yield stress of the single crystal and of the polycrystal are, respectively:
questions.keyExplanation: — | m = cos 20° cos 60° = 0.470 gives σ = 2/0.470 = 4.3 MPa, and the Hall–Petch term 0.7 × (0.0025)^(−1/2) = 14 MPa gives 50 + 14 = 64 MPa.
questions.detailed:
```
single crystal:  m = cos φ cos λ = 0.9397 × 0.5 = 0.470
                 σ_y = τ_crss / m = 2 / 0.470 = 4.26 ≈ 4.3 MPa
polycrystal:     d^(−1/2) = (0.0025 mm)^(−1/2) = 1/0.05 = 20 mm^(−1/2)
                 σ_y = σ₀ + k_y d^(−1/2) = 50 + 0.7 × 20 = 64 MPa
```
- (a) used d in **metres** with k_y in mm^(1/2): (2.5 × 10⁻⁶)^(−1/2) = 632 → 50 + 443 = 493 MPa — the classic unit slip.
- (b) doubles the Schmid result; (d) forgets σ₀ entirely.

The Schmid factor and the Hall–Petch coefficient are independent: orientation sets the single-crystal value, grain size sets the polycrystal increment.

questions.assertion: Twinning is the dominant mode of plastic deformation in FCC metals at room temperature.
questions.reason: FCC metals have only three independent slip systems, so twinning must supply the additional systems required by the von Mises criterion.

options.label: a
options.text: Both true, R correctly explains A

options.label: b
options.text: Both true, R does not explain A

questions.keyExplanation: — | Both statements are false: FCC has 12 slip systems and deforms mainly by slip, and it is HCP, not FCC, that is short of the five von Mises systems.
questions.concise: FCC has 12 slip systems and deforms mainly by slip; the three-system shortage belongs to HCP, not FCC.
questions.detailed:
- A is FALSE: FCC metals deform by **slip** at room temperature on 12 systems; twinning is occasional (annealing twins, shock loading, low-SFE alloys), never the dominant mode.
- R is FALSE: FCC has 4 {111} planes × 3 ⟨110⟩ directions = **12 ≥ 5** independent systems, so the von Mises criterion is satisfied without twinning.

Both statements transfer HCP's real problem onto FCC. **The pairing to fix:** HCP = 3 basal systems → needs twinning; FCC = 12 systems → slips freely; BCC = up to 48 → slips, but thermally activated at low T.

questions.text: Diffusion measurements for three solutes in the same host metal: solute I — D = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ m²/s at 800 K and 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ m²/s at 1000 K; solute II — 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ and 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ m²/s; solute III — 1.0 × 10⁻¹² and 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m²/s. Which reading of the data is correct?

options.label: a
options.text: Solute III has the largest activation energy, since its diffusivity rises by a factor of 100, the largest change of the three

options.label: b
options.text: Solute II has the largest activation energy, because its diffusivity is the highest at both temperatures

options.label: c
options.text: All three have equal activation energies, because the diffusivity rises with temperature in every case

options.label: d
options.text: Solute I has the largest activation energy, since its diffusivity rises by a factor of 1000 over the same interval, while solute II is the fastest at 800 K

questions.keyExplanation: — | Over the same temperature interval solute I's D rises by 10³ (the largest Q_d, ≈ 230 kJ/mol), while solute II has the highest D at 800 K.
questions.concise: Q_d ∝ ln(D₂/D₁) over the same ΔT, so solute I (10³ rise) has the largest Q_d, while solute II has the largest D at 800 K.
questions.detailed:
```
D₂/D₁ = exp[(Q/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂)] ,   1/800 − 1/1000 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹
Q = R ln(ratio) / 2.5 × 10⁻⁴
I:  ln 1000 = 6.91 → 230 kJ/mol     III: ln 100 = 4.61 → 153 kJ/mol
II:  ln 10   = 2.30 →  77 kJ/mol
```
- Fastest at a given temperature = **largest D at that temperature** = solute II (10⁻¹⁰ m²/s at 800 K) — not the one with the biggest Q_d.
- (a) reads the ratios in the wrong order; (c) confuses *fast* with *large Q_d*; (d) confuses "all increase with T" with "same Q_d" — on an Arrhenius plot only equal Q_d gives parallel lines.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about interfaces in a metal is/are correct?

statements.text: Grain-boundary atoms have abnormal coordination and unsatisfied bonding, so the boundary carries an excess energy per unit area.
Diffusion along grain boundaries has a lower activation energy than diffusion through the perfect lattice, so boundary transport dominates at low temperatures.
A coherent twin boundary has a much lower energy than a random high-angle grain boundary.
A coherent precipitate–matrix interface has a higher energy than a random high-angle grain boundary.

questions.keyExplanation: — | Items 1–3 are standard interface facts, but item 4 reverses the truth: coherent interfaces are low-energy, far below random high-angle boundaries.
questions.concise: Items 1–3 are standard interface facts; item 4 reverses the truth, since coherent interfaces are the low-energy ones.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: boundary atoms sit in distorted, wrongly coordinated positions, so the boundary carries excess energy (typically 0.3–0.8 J/m² for a random high-angle boundary).
- Item 2 — TRUE: Q_gb < Q_lattice, so the boundary/lattice diffusivity ratio **widens as T falls** — pipe and boundary paths dominate low-temperature transport.
- Item 3 — TRUE: a coherent twin boundary (a mis-stacked layer) has energy of order 0.02–0.05 J/m², far below a random high-angle boundary.
- Item 4 — FALSE: a **coherent** precipitate–matrix interface is the **lowest**-energy interface of the three; energy rises as coherency is lost (coherent → semi-coherent → incoherent).

questions.text: Applying the Hume-Rothery rules, which statement about solid solubility is correct?

options.label: a
options.text: C (0.077 nm) and Fe (0.124 nm) differ by about 38% in size, so carbon dissolves substitutionally in FCC iron — which is why austenite can hold about 2 wt% C

options.label: b
options.text: Ag (0.144 nm) and Pb (0.175 nm) are both FCC metals, so they dissolve completely in one another in the solid state

options.label: c
options.text: Zn (0.134 nm, HCP) and Cu (0.128 nm, FCC) differ by only about 5% in size with similar electronegativities, so they form a continuous solid solution

options.label: d
options.text: Cu (0.128 nm) and Ni (0.124 nm) differ by about 3% in size, have the same valence and similar electronegativities, and are both FCC, so they form a continuous solid solution

questions.keyExplanation: — | Cu–Ni satisfy every Hume-Rothery rule (about 3% size difference, same valence, similar electronegativity, both FCC) and are completely miscible.
questions.concise: Cu–Ni satisfy every Hume-Rothery rule (size, valence, electronegativity, structure) and are completely miscible.
questions.detailed: Cu and Ni satisfy the Hume–Rothery criteria: both are FCC, their atomic-size mismatch is about 3%, and their valence and chemical character are similar. They form a continuous solid solution. **(d)** is correct. Option (a) misclassifies carbon in iron as substitutional; (b) fails the size criterion; and (c) fails the same-crystal-structure criterion.

questions.text: Which combination of alloy type, phase-diagram feature and as-cast structure is correct?

options.label: a
options.text: A pure metal — a single invariant freezing point — its casting shows a broad mushy zone that is prone to hot tearing

options.label: b
options.text: An alloy of eutectic composition — one isothermal invariant reaction — a fine, uniform two-phase structure throughout the casting

options.label: c
options.text: An alloy of eutectic composition — freezing over a range of temperatures — primary dendrites surrounded by eutectic

options.label: d
options.text: An alloy just off the eutectic composition — one constant freezing temperature — no primary phase forms before the invariant reaction

questions.keyExplanation: — | A eutectic alloy freezes isothermally at the invariant temperature, so the whole casting is a fine, uniform two-phase eutectic with no primary phase.
questions.concise: A eutectic alloy freezes isothermally at one invariant temperature, giving a fine, uniform two-phase structure throughout.
questions.detailed: An alloy at the eutectic composition undergoes one isothermal invariant reaction: all remaining liquid transforms at the eutectic temperature into a fine, uniform two-phase eutectic structure. **(b)** is correct. Option (a) describes a pure metal, (c) incorrectly gives the eutectic alloy a freezing range and primary dendrites, and (d) describes neither the off-eutectic path nor the primary-phase formation correctly.

questions.text: During gas carburising the steel surface is held at 1.0 wt% C and the core starts at 0.1 wt% C. With D = 4 × 10⁻¹⁴ m²/s, after t = 10⁴ s the carbon content at x = 20 × 10⁻⁶ m is (erf 0.5 = 0.521, erf 1.0 = 0.843):
questions.detailed:
```
√(Dt) = √(4 × 10⁻¹⁴ × 10⁴) = √(4 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 2 × 10⁻⁵ m = 20 × 10⁻⁶ m
z = x / 2√(Dt) = 20 × 10⁻⁶ / (2 × 2 × 10⁻⁵) = 0.5
C = C₀ + (C_s − C₀)(1 − erf z)
  = 0.1 + (1.0 − 0.1)(1 − 0.521) = 0.1 + 0.431 = 0.53 wt%
```
- (a) 0.43 forgot to add C₀; (d) 0.57 used **+erf z** instead of **1 − erf z** (diffusion goes the wrong way); (b) 0.24 used z = x/√(Dt) — the factor 2 in z = x/2√(Dt) is the classic omission.

questions.text: Which combination of bonding, vacancy behaviour and diffusion consequence is correct?

options.label: a
options.text: A metal quenched from near its melting point retains its excess vacancies indefinitely at room temperature, because the vacancy concentration is fixed by the cooling rate rather than by temperature

options.label: b
options.text: Diffusion in a substitutional solid solution proceeds by direct atom–atom interchange, so no point defect is required and Q_d reflects only the energy needed to break bonds

options.label: c
options.text: Lead, held together by weaker metallic bonding than tungsten, must therefore have the higher vacancy formation energy and self-diffuse more slowly than tungsten at any given temperature

options.label: d
options.text: Tungsten, bonded much more strongly than lead, has the higher vacancy formation energy, so at a given absolute temperature its self-diffusion rate is far below that of lead

questions.keyExplanation: — | Strong metallic bonding in tungsten gives a large vacancy formation energy, so its self-diffusion rate at a given absolute temperature is far below lead's.
questions.concise: Strong bonding in tungsten means a large Q_f, so few vacancies form and D stays tiny; lead's weak bonding gives the opposite.
questions.detailed:
- (a) false — excess vacancies are **not** permanent: they migrate to sinks (surfaces, boundaries, dislocations) and anneal out; the equilibrium value depends only on temperature.
- (b) false — direct atom–atom interchange would require an entire plane of atoms to move at once; the **Kirkendall effect** (marker drift) is the proof that substitutional diffusion is vacancy-mediated.
- (c) false — it reverses the bonding order: weaker bonding in Pb means a **lower** Q_f and therefore **faster** self-diffusion.
- (d) TRUE — Q_f (and Q_m) scale with bond strength, so exp(−Q_f/kT) is astronomically smaller for W than for Pb at the same absolute T.

questions.text: Which statement(s) about cold work and annealing is/are correct?

statements.text: Strain hardening arises because the dislocation density rises during deformation and the dislocations increasingly impede one another's motion.
The stored energy of cold work — mainly the elastic strain energy of the dislocations — is the driving force for recovery and recrystallisation.
Recrystallisation proceeds without any nucleation, by the continuous rearrangement of the existing dislocation network into subgrain boundaries.
The recrystallisation temperature falls as the amount of prior cold work increases.

questions.keyExplanation: — | Item 3 reverses the truth: recovery is the continuous rearrangement of the existing dislocation network, whereas recrystallisation nucleates new strain-free grains.
questions.concise: Items 1, 2 and 4 are correct; item 3 describes recovery, not recrystallisation.
questions.detailed:
- Item 1 — TRUE: ρ climbs from about 10¹⁰ to 10¹⁵–10¹⁶ m⁻², and the forest of mutual obstacles is what raises the flow stress (τ ∝ Gb√ρ).
- Item 2 — TRUE: that stored elastic strain energy is the entire driving force for recovery and recrystallisation.
- Item 3 — FALSE: **recovery** is the continuous rearrangement of the existing network into subgrain boundaries; **recrystallisation** proceeds by **nucleation and growth** of new strain-free grains.
- Item 4 — TRUE: more cold work means more stored energy, so the driving force is reached at a **lower** temperature.

Item 3 is the misconception: recovery = rearrangement (no new grains), recrystallisation = new grains.
